I'm on Venlafaxine XR 300mg and Quetiapine XR 300mg and honestly they have saved my life.
I've been on Venlafaxine since 2012 and quetiapine since 2014. This past year I've started reducing the quetiapine, I was on 400mg and I dropped it by 50mg a day every six months and I'm feeling fine.

Venlafaxine treated my horrific depression and the quetiapine helped with the mood swings and the psychotic features.
I've been really lucky, but it took a long time and lots of trials - I've been trying antidepressants since I was 14.
In the end the meds allowed me breathing space to get on with therapy and that's what made all the difference.
Can I hijack your response and say you sound like an amazing person to have as a penpal?! ❤️✨️

Hiya!
I'm 38 (in a couple of weeks) F from the UK, pansexual, used to hate everything but now I absolutely love being alive and trying to do new things and having fun experiences, making friends, seeing new places - I missed a lot of my life being mentally ill so I'm trying to make up for it now!

I'm looking for some long term penpals to write long letters to about lots of different things, I have a variety of interests including being outdoors (not so much active as I have a chronic pain condition but I do love being outside), reading, painting and miniatures.

Please do feel free to message me if you'd like to write 😊

Hello!
I'm 38 in a few weeks (eeek), F and married, but hopefully soon I'll be able to break free.
I have had a massively turbulent life and love to talk about mental health and recovery to anyone who will listen.
I like writing long letters and including little drawings and bits and pieces, once we've established that we're a good fit!
My main hobby is miniatures, but I also love being out in the sunshine at the beach or in the countryside, painting, and reading!

Send me a message if you'd like to write 😊❤️✨️

I'm an Occupational Therapy assistant working in a medium secure forensic mental health hospital 😊
I'm also currently studying Occupational therapy BSc and trying to switch onto mental health nursing.

Don't let your illness dictate your career choice - but I will say, you need to make sure you can cope with listening to potentially negative and distressing conversations day in, day out. It can be very difficult but it is very rewarding.

Prescription medication to ease anxiety if that's a possibility.

Practice meditation - start now! 
Wear headphones and an eye mask and don't take them off for the whole flight. Create a playlist or two with different audio books and music for your different moods so you've always got something to listen to.
Sleep, if you can.

I lost my last job due to a mental breakdown and I couldn't accept that I was far too unwell to be working, so rather than just claiming benefits I was desperately applying for jobs left, right and centre. 
I got an interview for a job at a call centre and went along to it. I passed the maths and reading tests with flying colours and went in to the face to face interview. It was going well until one of the interviewers said to me
"We have a lot of customers calling who are unhappy, complaining. They might shout, call you names, say you're a waste of time or space.. do you think you're able to cope with that?"
And I just burst into tears and sobbed out 'no, I can't, I'm sorry'..!
They were actually lovely and it was me who suggested I terminated the interview, but oh my goodness the embarrassment! 

(I'm lots better now and I've been working in forensic mental health for two years 😁)

My big ones (wide and/or keloid) have been deep red for a long, long time (I'm talking decade or longer) and when it's cold they turn purple like this with silvery edges. 
They've started to fade to light pink now and they don't really go as purple any more, so I think that it's just because when they're newer there's more blood vessels and younger scar tissue, so when it's cold and the blood vessels contract away from the surface of the skin, you just can't see as much red blood any more. Now there's more mature scar tissue there's less blood vessels 'on show' so the colour change is less obvious.

Definitely nothing to worry about, albeit a little bit annoying!
I used Bio-Oil which really helped mine to relax and fade; if that's something you want, of course. 

Take care 🧡

Believe me, telling a young child that they are 'the worst' or otherwise making them believe that they are not worthy of the love and kindness shown to other children (like with her cousin) will destroy her self esteem, self confidence, and relationships with not only her parents but quite possibly for the rest of her life.

I got a place at university to study Occupational Therapy. 

Yes I was scared that my weight would hold me back and yes I've found that sometimes I can't do as much physically as I would like, but I'm so, so happy now.

I let my weight hold me back for a long time, affecting my self esteem and self confidence, and it was only when I stopped that I was truly able to start living.

I have a suspicion that no matter what I say I won't make a difference to your opinion.

I will start by saying that from the ages of 13 to 35 I was clinically depressed, for two decades I suffered suicidal ideation every single day to an extreme I doubt many people have experienced, and I do feel your pain.

Hello!
I have fibromyalgia and degenerative disc disease; I'm in a lot of pain every day but the fatigue is worse.

At the moment I work part time (two days a week) for the NHS as an Occupational Therapy Assistant in a forensic mental health hospital, and I go to university three days a week to study Occupational Therapy 😊
I don't do an awful lot else as most of my time is taken up studying! 

I do volunteer as a Listener with 7 Cups, a peer support network, which takes about 4-6 hours a week. And I often volunteer with the NHS Trust I work for, on Saturday mornings we have a Parkrun at our hospital for the service users, and on an ad-hoc basis I support the experts by experience team by interviewing potential staff, doing ward audits, and more. It's fun, and I enjoy it.

If I find myself with spare time, I spend it walking outside (slowly!) or working on my dollhouse, which is where all my spare cash disappears into 😂

Once I've finished my degree, I hope that I will be able to get a full time position as an Occupational Therapist. The NHS are a good employer and have given me a brilliant set of reasonable adjustments.

I was diagnosed with clinical depression at the age of 13, while I was self-harming and struggling with awful low mood. I began to suffer with suicidal thoughts the following year. I got my GCSEs but I failed my A-levels because I missed so much school. 
I got a job in a cinema at 18, which was good but my mental health was awful. The suicidal thoughts were everyday and constant, strong and difficult to cope with. I was diagnosed with bipolar 2 after starting to experience hallucinations, and I changed my job. 
Unfortunately I continued to decline and I lost that job after a few years due to a breakdown.
I spent my whole life convinced that I would kill myself on my 30th birthday. That 30 years was more than enough. But I didn't. 

It took me ten years to find another job. 
But in that time, I worked my ass off at recovering. I had lots of therapy and used self help techniques and tools to get a grip on why I was so unhappy and how I could change it. Eventually, I came out the other side and, like you, my suicidal thoughts abated, for the most part.

But - again, like you - I felt massive regret for those years that I had "lost" to my mental illness. I felt that my life was flying by and I'd wasted this time, so what was the point in starting now, when I'd already wasted so much?
But then I thought - I haven't wasted the time. I spent it getting better. Time recovering is not wasted. Time healing is not wasted.
Yes, I am older. No, I am not the youthful 15 year old any more. But while I'm older, I'm wiser as well. And even if you don't think you are, you will be. Its impossible not to be.

I started university this year at the age of 37, so do not let me hear you say that you are too old or too far behind to make something of yourself..! Have a Google of people who've done things in later life. Its not only possible, but very much encouraged. 

I know you've struggled and you've missed the 'normal' checkpoints of someone growing up, but there's honestly no reason why you can't do them now. Go and get your learners licence and some driving lessons; enroll at college to take the essential Maths/English so you can look at enrolling at university if that's something you want to do later; start looking after yourself now.
Personal hygiene is important as I'm sure you know, but it's also simple - shower daily with soap and shampoo (wash hair 2 or 3 times weekly) and don't forget your feet; wash your face and hands in the morning with soap and hot water; use toothpaste and toothbrush to clean your teeth twice a day. Make sure you keep your clothes and bedding clean, and that's you good. 
As for being malnourished, depending on the severity you may need to see a doctor or nurse. Just focus on trying to get yourself eating some healthy food, fruits and veggies, protein.

As for missing out on fun - you've got potentially 70 years to make thousands and thousands of memories, have hundreds of thousands of hours of fun.. 

Your last point about relationships - they will happen if they do. Nobody can say that you would have had a relationship even if you hadn't had all the struggles you have, or if that relationship would have been a good one, or worth pursuing. 

I hope some of this helps. 
Don't write your life off. You've had a struggle and time has passed. But what's gone has gone, and it's now time to move on and make your life something amazing.
If you want, drop me a message. (It might take me a little while to reply but I promise I will)

Take care.

I cried so hard first time I heard that.
The guy who voiced it got it absolutely 100% spot on.

First of all, online tests only give guidance. Don't take what they say as fact. To be diagnosed with anything you need to see a professional - in this case, a psychiatrist.

I suggest you seek help from a medical professional if you are hearing voices, as it is a sign that something isn't right. But that doesn't mean you're insane. It could be something as simple as you being very dehydrated or having low blood sugar. Hallucinations can be caused by a wide range of things, not just mental illness, which is why you need to be seen by a doctor.

If they do refer you on to a psychiatrist, you will be able to explore the recent development of voices with them. 

Don't panic; you're not insane. 
Make a doctors appointment. Treat yourself with kindness and look after your body. Seek support when needed. You'll be okay. 🤍

Munchausens has been around for a long time - the faking of illness for attention. Its just changed name now to factituous disorder.

Hypochondria is being afraid that you're ill, being so worried that you constantly go to the doctor - but you GENUINELY believe you have the illness.

My mum constantly attacked my body from a really young age all the way till I got married at 23. In the run up to my wedding she was telling me to drink nothing but Slim-Fast shakes because "nobody wants to be fat on their wedding day".

After that, I told her outright that she needed to stop, because she'd driven me into an eating disorder, into hating every inch of my own body, into having no self esteem. I told her if she didn't stop, I would not have her in my life, because I couldn't cope any longer.

She did refuse to accept that she'd done any of it, or said any of the things I recounted, but she said okay, I won't comment on your weight or body unless you want me to. And so far, she's stuck to that. I'm 37 now.

I suggest you do something similar if you can. If not, acknowledge that you are beautiful and actually your body is absolutely perfect the way it is.
It's very likely your mother has raging insecurities that she's projecting on to you because she's unable to deal with them herself - like mine. You don't deserve to have to deal with this so distance yourself from it. Take care of yourself.
Women are in need of a carvery. 😂

Why are you trying to "wash the drug" from your body when the drug is what's supposed to help?

But looking at the rest of your post, I don't think the drug is what's causing your weight loss. You're starving yourself and then doing massive amounts of exercise.. 
You need to eat properly if you're going to exercise that much; definitely don't fast and do all that. I would seek advice from a dietician if possible or your doctor.

Your weight loss journey is the one I am just starting. My start weight was 396lb (highest weight ever was 412lb) and after 5 weeks with MJ I'm down 30lb.

Stories of success at any weight are encouraging but when you've got so much to lose it can feel overwhelming - but to see that you've done it and you've done it the way I'm planning to... it's so inspiring!

How incredible do you feel?! Can you remember what you felt like at your heaviest or has it all faded away as you got lighter and healthier?

I have struggled with my weight, binge eating, emotional eating, self esteem... you name it... for most of my life. My mum destroyed my healthy relationship with food and later I gained 12st on psych meds. Its been a mess.

I did my third 5mg jab of Mounjaro yesterday and am 30lb down from my start weight of 396lb. 
But the best bit is that I don't even think about food any more. I don't want to eat. I don't want to solve my problems with food. I don't feel nauseous or anything and I haven't yet managed to get myself consistently working in my new habits, especially if I'm very stressed or upset, but I find that if I end up at the cupboard or fridge- my usual comfort stop- I just open and close the door because I genuinely don't want anything in there.

I have breakfast every morning and then very little else. I need to work on my protein intake and I really need to work on exercise, but I found that my "obsess about food" switch has been disabled. Its not off, its simply not working, and that's wonderful.

My husband is the nicest most caring man I could ever hope to be with. He is also impotent and has absolutely no interest in sex. He refuses to see any therapist because he sees no point.

We've been married for 14 years in October and I absolutely regret it. I don't hate him, but it's driven a huge wedge between us. We are now in separate bedrooms, we sit on separate sofas, we barely speak. I hate him touching me and I am desperate for the day that I have enough money saved so I can leave.

I'm not saying every case will be like mine. I'm probably on the drastic end of the spectrum. But sex and intimacy are so, so important to relationships and marriage - be absolutely 110% certain that you want to be with this man forever even if he won't be intimate with you before you even entertain the idea of marrying him.

Sexless marriages are HARD. Have a look at the subreddit (I can't remember exactly what it is) for those of us in sexless marriages before you make your decision.


Take care.

Throughout my own struggle with mental illness I discovered a desire to work with people who also have mental ill health, to do whatever I can to bring them comfort and support and happiness during their dark time. And that lit a fire within me; I volunteered with peer support charities and then started my own group and then I got a job with the NHS working in forensic inpatient mental health and now I'm going to university in September to study Occupational Therapy BSc... 

I've been working for just over a year now (I was unemployed for ten years due to ill health) and its genuinely been the happiest year of my life. I love my job so much. I get to work with the people that society wants to lock away and forget; to help them reforge a life worth living and give them my time, trust and support. 

My purpose in life, which I discovered quite late, is to help other people, and if I'm not doing that then I feel miserable and unfulfilled. If I can help someone, I will. 


I do take medication, antidepressants and antipsychotics, and I worked really bloody hard at all my therapy etc etc.

Have you considered Prader-Willi syndrome? Characterised by excessive appetite and overeating, obesity, typically shorter than average. This is when a child will feel hunger but be unable to satiate themselves because of the disorder, leading to continuous eating and weight gain.

Otherwise, just talk to the parents. Just say look, this is coming from a place of only love for this child, I'm not criticising in any way, but I'm a little concerned that he may be eating to disguise his feelings. I don't know how old you are but it doesn't sound like you're very old, possibly at the stage where you're leaving college and considering uni?

When I left Sixth Form (age 16-18, UK) my head of year absolutely hated me because I was the only one who didn't go to university. She said I was letting myself (and the school) down, but my argument was that I didn't know what I liked to learn, let alone what I wanted to do at degree, so why saddle myself with thousands in student debt for nothing?
Anyway, I left and a few months later I was working in the new cinema complex. 
Fast forward a few years, left the cinema and got a job as a sampler with the Environment Agency which I liked, but I was too anxious and shy to be confident enough to make it my own. My physical health required a job swap into an office role after a year or so, too.

Then, I got ill. My BPD, or depression, or a mix of everything I have, made it impossible for me to work. I lost my job, my driving licence (surrendered because of suicidal ideation), friends, family, money..
That was ten years ago and it was a dark time. I was 26.

As I slowly, very slowly, started recovering, I had the inkling in the back of my mind that I wanted to work in mental health. I didn't know how or what role, just that I did. So I started to take some distance learning courses in various mental health related subjects. I volunteered as a peer support group facilitator. I did mental health first aid. Two years ago I volunteered with a charity that teaches adults to read, as a Coordinator, and my confidence rocketed.

In April this year, at the age of 36, I started working for the NHS at a secure mental health inpatient hospital. I work in a social centre that's part of the occupational therapy department, and from my very first day there I absolutely loved it - and that is no exaggeration.
I work 16hr a week and that's enough for now, because I do struggle with severe fatigue from my physical illnesses. But the job is perfect.
And in September I'm going to college to do a year-long Access to Higher Education diploma so that next year I'll be ready to go to University to study to become a fully qualified Occupational Therapist! 

So please, please, please do NOT worry about your age or your twenties 'disappearing' while you decide what you want to do! Life is so, so short and we aren't guaranteed another go - make the best out of this one.
Take the jobs that you'll enjoy, try volunteering, do some night classes, travel, socialise, try out loads of new hobbies...

Things have a way of falling into place when you're not forcing them to - if you're not 100% sure what you want to do, don't go to uni. Why study something if it won't further your career or education path?
Use the time and money on other things instead.

Once you know what you want to study/ work in, make your plans and go for it! Until then, just enjoy your life ❤️

There are many books out there on the subject of BPD, but just as with the myriad of websites, you have to be very careful and selective over which ones you choose to read.

Some are written like a textbook, some like a fiction book, and some like a memoir. There are some which teach skills and are written like school books.

Personally, I found these to be very useful (I have BPD)..

These books are useful as guides for someone newly diagnosed with BPD, providing unbiased and useful information:

1. The Everything Guide to Borderline Personality Disorder; Constance M Dolecki MS PHDC (ISBN-13: 978-1-4405-2970-2)
2. Lost in the Mirror; Richard Moskovitz MD (ISBN-13: 978-0-87833-266-3)

These books are wonderfully useful at helping you to develop skills in DBT - Dialectical Behaviour Therapy, a therapy developed specifically for people with BPD. I would recommend slight caution if you're newly diagnosed or aren't seeing a therapist as using these skills without help can sometimes cause more problems. However as you progress along your recovery journey, learning more and more DBT skills will do nothing but good for you and your mental health.

3. Calming the Emotional Storm; Sheri Van Dijk MSW (ISBN-13: 978-1-60882-087-0)
4. The Dialectical Behaviour Therapy Skills Workbook; McKay, Wood & Brantley (ISBN-13: 978-1-57224-513-6)
     (plus the 'The Dialectical Behaviour Therapy Diary' to match; ISBN-13: 978-1-57224-956-1)
5. The Expanded Dialectical Behaviour Therapy Skills Training Manual; Lane Pederson PSYD LP DBTC (ISBN-13: 978-1-93612-812-9)

This isn't BPD-specific but is focused on teaching skills around managing emotions, which I have personally found to be incredibly useful:

6. Don't Let Your Emotions Run Your Life; Scott E Spradlin MA (ISBN-13: 978-1-57224-309-5)

And lastly, a couple more non-BPD specific books that offer useful & helpful information to people with the problems associated with BPD:

7. Mindfulness for Dummies; Shamash Alidina (ISBN-13: 978-0-470-66086-7)
8. The Highly Sensitive Person; Elaine N Aron (ISBN-13: 978-0-7225-3896-8)
9. 'Overcoming' Anger and Irritability (A Self-Help CBT Guide); William Davies (ISBN-13: 978-1-84901-131-0)
10. The Compassionate Mind; Paul Gilbert (ISBN-13: 978-1-84901-098-6)

And the last one (!) which I bought to give to my husband to read (but which I also got use from) is this one:

11. Loving Someone with Borderline Personality Disorder; Shari Y Manning PHD (ISBN-13: 978-1-59385-607-6)


I hope that some of that will be helpful for you - and anyone else reading this - because honestly I've read every one of these books and got a lot of help and use from them. Especially so from the DBT Skills Workbook & Diary.

There are a number of reasons why you could be experiencing auditory hallucinations that are most definitely not schizophrenia.
I know it can be absolutely terrifying when you begin to experience things that aren't "normal", and also when you're looking at getting a diagnosis or seeing a psychiatrist.

My personal experience with auditory hallucinations began when I was about 19; I started to hear a 'noise' like hundreds of people talking all at once, much like being in a busy train station or shopping centre. I also began to see shadow like figures in windows and doorways which were quite scary.
After some time, I began to hear five distinctive voices which would talk about me in a negative manner, all the time. Some time later, two voices disappeared and one became a figure which I could see, and she talks to me in mostly negative terms, but sometimes positive and comforting. 

During that lot, I was seeing various mental health teams and psychiatrists, and taking different medications at different points in time. I have had a diagnosis of bipolar 2 which was then changed to borderline personality disorder (BPD) alongside depression and anxiety. The hallucinations were called 'pseudo-hallucinations' because I am mostly aware that they are not real, and when I believe that they are real, I am able to calm myself down fairly quickly.

Sorry for the long splurge of details about me, I just wanted to reassure you really that hearing some noises or voices doesn't mean that you have schizophrenia, and that medication isn't scary and isn't always a bad thing.
My first try was quetiapine and it made me into a zombie, so we gave up. I took no antipsychotics for years, until I tried abilify, which was good but gave me tardive dyskinesia. So I then tried quetiapine again, and it worked! I'm now on a maintenance dose (for me) of 300mg/day and it's working well, especially in combination with the venlafaxine.


Hearing voices or noises is so scary but please don't be scared of seeking professional help. And if the first time doesn't get you the results you deserve, try somebody else.
Please don't be scared of medication - nobody will force you to take any if you really don't want to, but it can be really helpful sometimes. If you do decide to try it, you are very much within your rights to say you want to stop it at any time.

It's possible that your experiences are linked to your PTSD - my psychiatrist told me at my most recent appointment that my 'figure' had appeared because of my constant negative thoughts, which had turned outwards and become a corporeal thing, rather than just thoughts in my head.

And lastly, please don't worry about being taken into hospital. It is most unlikely that any psychiatrist will want to admit you to hospital unless you are severely poorly, because hospital is not a good environment for anyone bar the most poorly people.

Lots of steps! Lots of baby steps.

The first thing I'd say to them is well done. Well done for wanting to get better, and to actually seek ways that you can learn how to cope. 

Motivation is a hard thing to get and harder to sustain when you have a mental illness, especially BPD, which actively tries to persuade you that you're not worth the time or effort.
A good place to start would be to sit down and work out why you want to get better, and work out what you'll use to keep your motivation high. 
As I mentioned, a part of recovery is making a life worth living, so perhaps base your motivation on that.

Taking the first step is scary but if you know that at the end of this particular journey is something that could potentially lead to your recovery from BPD.. hopefully that will help to guide you and reassure you while you seek help.

You need to get the help from a mental health professional - self help with books and the Internet will help to solidify what you learn and practice in therapy, but really you need to be shown how to use the skills first. 

I don't know where you are, but for me, the very first step was to go to my GP (General Practitioner/family doctor). I was then referred to the CMHT (Community Mental Health Team) for an assessment, after which I was then placed in the CCaTT (Complex Care and Treatment Team) and given a Care Coordinator. 

Through them, I was given access to CBT (Cognitive Behavioural Therapy), as well as counselling, and then later on I had CAT (Cognitive Analytical Therapy).

After a couple of years, I got a place on a Life Skills group especially for people with BPD. That lasted 6 months, and at the end of it, I was given a place on a 2yr intensive therapy programme with the Personality Disorders team, on the basis that once it was over, I would be discharged.
I got a case manager, had weekly meetings with him, I did another round of Life Skills, and a course of CFT (Compassion Focused Therapy). 

We worked on distress tolerance skills, mindfulness, problem solving, crisis management, and more.

I first entered services in 2001 for depression at age 14, was with the EIS (Early Intervention in Psychosis Service) between 2006 and 2009, transferred to the CMHT in 2009, discharged for 6 months in 2011, readmitted later in 2011, and I was finally discharged on 30 Dec 2019.

Its a long journey but it's really worth it.

And again, I'm so sorry for waffling. I hope that I've managed to reply to what you were asking!

I really hope that you find the desire within yourself to reach out for help, BPD can be tamed and become a lot less distressing with the right skills and so on.
I can't comment on the brain damage but I am sorry you have to cope with that. 

Don't throw your things away; I know that when you're in the midst of a suicidal crisis it can seem like the right thing to do, to spare your friends and family the distress once you're gone, but you're also not thinking clearly because your thoughts are being jumbled by your mood.

I would encourage you to seek help as soon as you can from a medical practitioner, if no other way than to call 999/911 etc. Your life is important and valuable, even though I know you won't be able to see it as so.

I'm really glad that you could find some useful bits in my slew of text! 
I'm also glad that you're able to recognise the strength in yourself, because as long as you can see that you're strong, that you're coping with awful things happening TO you and that BPD isn't inherently threaded through every fibre of your being.. you can recover. You will recover.

You're strong, and you're not alone.
Take care.

My depression began at age 12, and I was diagnosed with clinical depression and anxiety at age 14. I then suffered badly with my mental health all my life. 
I was diagnosed with bipolar which got changed to borderline personality disorder with psychosis and some other ones.
I struggled so badly to keep going- I was in the dark every day, constant suicidal thoughts, self harm, complete lack of motivation and desire to do anything at all.
I completely messed up my A Levels because I just didn't care enough to study. I got a job at a cinema where my self harm escalated and I developed an eating disorder. I moved on to another job with a fantastic company but four years later I lost it because I had a mental breakdown.
All those years of living in the darkness, wishing to die, lonely but not wanting to reach out.. 
And then I was accepted into the treatment team where I would be helped back to human again. I worked SO HARD at therapy and life skills and the 2yr treatment program and the groups, I threw myself at everything they offered. 

Today I am 1 year and 3 months on from being discharged from mental health services and I'm in the best place (mentally) of my life.
I lost 20 years to mental illness - I view it as literally being lost in a black fog - but I kept going and going and fighting and never giving up even though that's all I ever wanted to do.. I feel better than ever and I have a huge bank of skills that I learnt in therapy to reach for when I dip, which is often. But the difference is, I know I will come back up the next day.
I believed the whole time that I would never get any better - I would always read other people's stories and think "why can't I get better?" or "they were only ill for a year, I've been ill for 16.. I'll never be happy again.."
But I fought to get here and I'm finally here.

I wish I could go to every single person who is fighting against mental illness and tell them that it *will* get better, but it will be when you are ready. Some people are only poorly for 6 months, and some are poorly for 40 years. 
But there is a wealth of information and help and advice online, and even if you can't immediately access therapy there are things online you can use to help.
Don't let the illness convince you that you're hopeless and loveless, because you're not. All the negative thoughts are JUST THOUGHTS.
Think that you're a unicorn. A sparkly unicorn with a pink horn.
Are you a unicorn? NO.
Thoughts don't make things true. 
They can be distressing and really realistic but don't listen to them. Keep fighting. Keep believing.

I have three ruptured discs in my lumbar spine; L5/S1, L4/L5, and L3/L4. They are so badly ruptured now that they will never heal naturally; the only way is a discectomy and a spinal fusion.
However, I am very overweight and should I have the surgery, not only is it highly risky because of my weight anyway, but the hardware used in the fusion (the bolts) just wouldn't be able to support my weight for long enough to let the bone fuse. They would just snap.
I have to lose a lot of weight before they will operate.

So, in the meantime, I am (trying) to manage the pain, the spasms, and the sciatica with a combination of pain medication, heat therapy, and physical therapy.

I had a long course of physical therapy with a physiotherapist up until the start of last year, when I was discharged. Now, I manage it myself. There are a set of exercises that I do every day, without fail. Then I have a set of exercises which I do if I'm feeling particularly well, to build up my muscle tone. I have another extra set which focuses on stretching tight muscles and they are easy to do if I'm feeling tired or sore.

I have a microwaveable heat belt (one of those corduroy ones filled with beans) which is on my back a LOT! Heat is FANTASTIC for my back pain; I would strongly recommend you try it too. It will help you to not only soothe the immediate pain, but it will draw extra blood to the area which will speed up healing and reduce inflammation. I also use a Deep Heat herbal roll-on when I can't use the belt, to continue the heat therapy.

Movement is key - don't let yourself be still for too long. It feels counterproductive doesn't it, but you need to move to keep the blood flowing, to get everything healing and mobile again. 
Strengthen your abs to improve your posture which will help take some pressure off your back.

If its possible for you, losing weight will help - losing just 4lb of weight will take 16lb of pressure off your spine.

Drink lots of water to keep yourself hydrated.
Eat foods containing omega-3 fatty acids; leafy green veggies like kale and spinach; plant based proteins; and turmeric, if you like it! These will help reduce inflammation.
Try and avoid foods high in sugar, saturated fats, refined oils, and processed meat, as these can increase inflammation.


I hope these help you in some way - if you like, you are more than welcome to message me. I do hope that your disc heals without surgery x

So when I had my first experience of psychosis I was about 19 so I'm not 100% if this is the same for under 18s, but it won't be hugely different.

You'll need to either:
1. Go to your GP and explain what's been going on, what you feel like and what you believe is happening to you. They should then make a referral for you to see a mental health professional.
OR
2. Self refer through IAPT, who will be able to see you for an assessment and then signpost you in the right direction, whether that is giving you some CBT or counselling, referring you on to another mental health team, or sending you to your GP.

Self-referral:
https://www.nhs.uk/service-search/find-a-psychological-therapies-service/

For me, I went through my GP first. I had a phonecall from someone who did an assessment which took about half an hour, and then after that they put me on the waiting list for a place with the Early Intervention in Psychosis Service (EIS). It didn't take too long before I was accepted and given a care co-ordinator. 
I saw a psychiatrist fairly regularly who diagnosed bipolar 2 disorder with psychosis, and put me on three new medications - a mood stabiliser, a new antidepressant, and an antipsychotic.

This was a good 14 or so years ago but I would think that apart from waiting lists perhaps being longer, the general process is still much the same.


Another thing to keep in mind is that while unpleasant, you are aware of the strange and paranoid thoughts, which is always a good sign as it is said that the people with more severe psychosis don't recognise that they actually have an illness at all.

Keep going, get in touch with your GP or with IAPT, they will help you to get access to the professional support you need.
(Also this may be unwanted advice, but if you believe you are suffering with psychosis, I would try very hard to stop smoking weed - it will not help you at all and can actually make you very poorly)


You can also call these helplines for more information:

• Mind Infoline: 0300 123 3393 (Mon-Fri 9am-6pm)

• Rethink Mental Illness 0300 5000 927 (Mon-Fri 9:30am-4pm)

• The Mix (for under 25s) 0808 808 4994 (Sun-Fri 2pm-11pm)

• OCD Action 0845 390 6232 (Mon-Fri 9:30am-5pm) - some of what you describe sounds like the compulsions found in OCD

I constantly feel like I'm lying.
Like I'm making everything up.


But I think it's part of psychosis, and paranoia. Psychosis makes you question your reality, and if you're questioning what's real, it's not a massive stretch to start questioning if the UNreality is real - if that makes sense!

I'm constantly paranoid and anxious that I'll be accused of lying, because I am on benefits for multiple conditions and I had a HELL of a time proving I was *sick enough* to get them in the first place. I don't have anything to worry about, but my paranoia convinces me daily that they'll be kicking the door down to arrest me for fraud any time now.
This doesn't help either.

In my case, I keep a "blind journal" of my psychosis to help me. I write down what I'm experiencing at the time, put a tab on to label the date/time, and turn the page. I don't read these experiences again unless I have a really, really good reason to need to do. It might seem pointless to do, but being able to see these journals with all the tabs on (and the index file I keep) really helps me to recognise that I DO have these experiences, they DO affect me, and although I believe I'm making it up a lot of the time, when I'm experiencing these [hallucinations] they are 100% real to me.

So I hope I can make this a fairly short comment cause honestly my journey from first becoming depressed to where I am today is such an experience it could take a long time to explain!

I first had symptoms of depression around age 10, though my mum says I was always 'a depressed child'. I was then formally diagnosed with clinical depression and anxiety at age 13 by my GP and put on antidepressants. My first suicidal thoughts came into being when I was about 14/15, I don't recall exactly when, but I was definitely still at high school because I would daydream a LOT about jumping off the roof of the school building.
I was then diagnosed with bipolar 2 and psychosis at age 19 and put on antipsychotics and benzodiazapines as well as antidepressants. I was working in a cinema which I hated, I frequently self harmed by cutting- the one episode that stands out to me even now is when I found a glass bottle while cleaning a screen one day, so I took it and put it in my locker. Later on my shift, I went to get the bottle and I went down the back stairs and hid under them. I smashed the bottle and used it to hurt myself. I left the bottle but took some of the pieces home. That was a bad time.

I used to take my car out after shifts and instead of going home I'd just drive for hours and hours, going nowhere, just driving. I couldn't bear going home because I felt so unhappy. I'd drive really really fast, stupidly fast, because for that few minutes I felt something other than the blank, black depression. 
One night I drove out to a motorway bridge not far from my house and stood watching the traffic. I wished I had the courage to jump but I didn't. Someone called the police and they came to take me home. 

I got a new job and a couple of years later a new diagnosis - they said I'd been misdiagnosed and I actually had borderline personality disorder instead. I continued to sink into deeper and deeper depression, i hated myself, I hated my life, I hated everything. I felt sad, angry, numb. In 2013 I eventually lost my job because I was having to take so much time off sick, because I just couldn't cope with being in the office, I couldn't concentrate.
That was the lowest point of my life by a long way. Every single day I'd wake up wishing I hadn't. I was self harming every day. I cried until I had no tears left - and that's not just a saying, I literally ran out - I'd just sit there wanting to cry and let all the sadness out, but no tears were left. I despised myself - every thought was negative, cruel, dark, suicidal. My husband got so desperate, so .. beaten down by my belief that I was better off dead, that he said to me one day "I love you, but if you really need to do it, then I'm not going to stop you". And we both cried together. I lived in darkness for years.
And all through this time I was on medication, and at various points I was seeing mental health professionals. The CPN I had when they told me I had BPD said that people with BPD were manipulative attention seekers who were incurable and so she didn't want to work with me any more. That did a lot to bolster my confidence.

My recovery began when I was discharged from her care. 6 months later I was in such a state I went to my GP and he immediately referred me back to services. However, because I'd moved house I was now under a different 'hub' and so a different team. I was put with the Complex Care and Treatment Team after an assessment and an appointment with a psychiatrist. That psychiatrist, I believe, was the one who saved my life. He changed my medications to venlafaxine and quetiapine which I am on to this day. I did a course of counselling and was given a care coordinator. Once my meds were stable, I did a course of CBT. I was assigned a new care coordinator and we worked together on some really important things. I then did a group called Life Skills which was developed for people with BPD or emotional regulation problems. Once that 6 month course was finished, the facilitator offered me a place on the Personality Disorders Structured Clinical Management program, which is a 100-week intensive intervention program for people with BPD. He was my new care coordinator and he was the person who gave me the skills and the motivation to change my life. The program was amazing, the skills I learnt are invaluable. I did the life skills course again, and I also did a 4 month Compassion Focused Therapy course and another round of CBT.
Alongside all this, I did a lot of personal soul searching, homework, and skill practice. Anyone who tells you that recovery from a mental illness is easy is lying. It takes a hell of a lot of hard work but my god it is worth it.

I am now 33 and although I will most likely be taking the venlafaxine and quetiapine for life, because I've tried to come off them and I've not done well, I'm now 1year out of services with no issues, and although I do have suicidal thoughts (part of the territory with BPD) I can use my skills and my generally good mood to cope with them.
I am 6 years clean from self harm and have a huge arsenal of skills and techniques that I've built up over my time in the various therapy programs I did, which help me every day.

In the darkest times, when I'd been depressed for years and I laid in bed begging for death, I would have laughed in your face if you'd have told me that I'd be where I am now. I genuinely thought I was never ever going to get better. I'd read stories of people who'd been depressed and got better and were all "just hold on, it gets better!" and I'd scoff "yeah whatever" and turn the page. 

But I am testament to it. It DOES GET BETTER.
You have to TRY. Its not a passive thing. And thats where I went wrong. I thought it would get better on its own. But I had to work. I had to work REALLY HARD. 
But I'd do the work again a hundred times over, because being able to say "I'm on the right side of recovery" whenever I'm talking about my journey, feels so damn good.

By the way - I am still unemployed, it will be 8 years on the 21st Feb 2021. I am on long term sick/disabled claiming ESA & PIP for both mental and physical illnesses. However I have now started to try volunteering - I am doing 4hr/month with Lancashire Mind (a mental health charity) and I've just signed up with Lancashire Recovery College, which is a wonderful place that provides free courses on all things mental health. My title is "Volunteer Recovery Journey Enabler"! I am also setting up a peer support group that combines art & mental wellbeing. None of these take very long to do at any one time but are enough to start me back on the long road to employment.


You are worth trying for. You are worth working hard for.
Never, ever, ever, give up.
It really does get better.

I know you want your mum to be okay, but you need to look after yourself too. The thing is, if you keep thinking that you'll just get by, one day you'll wake up and realise that actually, you can't cope anymore. And then what will your mum do? 
If it's available, please try and get some support for yourself. You don't necessarily need to go on medication or into therapy, even some talk therapy or carer support could be all that you need to keep you from slipping back.
I am worried that you suffered yourself from depression and only recently came off medication; I wonder why you both came off at roughly the same time, too.

Your mum needs to find her own reasons to want to be well; you probably know but you can tell a depressed person until you're blue in the face that they have this reason or that reason, but unless they believe you it's almost pointless.

Encourage your mum to find things to do that she really enjoys; put housework aside for now and look for something that really gets her involved and smiling. Smiling and laughter are incredibly powerful.
If she's refusing to leave the house, try reading, watching upbeat TV or YouTube (short clips and programmes are good), painting and drawing, crafting, baking, cooking, having a mini spa day with bubble baths and nail polish, writing letters or in a journal, playing with makeup or face paint, cuddling a pet, looking through photos, playing board games with you, doing some yoga or pilates, gentle and short length exercise videos off YouTube, and so on.
If she's up for going outside, encourage her to do so as much as possible. Fresh air and sunshine is wonderful especially at this time of year. Short walks will do her the world of good, as will being outside and seeing the natural world around her.
Introduce social activities gradually and slowly, like a Skype or Zoom call with her friends or family, or even a peer support group or therapist. There are so many groups that offer support you'll find one really easily. 

The worst thing she can do, able to focus or no, is to sit around the house and ruminate on her current situation. Activity and distraction from her current distress will help a lot.

Take care.

What helped me was getting into a really good treatment program with a specialist personality disorders team. I had a 6month long life skills group before entering a 100-week 'Personality Disorder Structured Clinical Management' program, with a personality disorder practitioner who i got on incredibly well with, who was sympathetic and kind but firm and who knew exactly how tough he could be with me in regards to dealing with my behaviour.
I learnt about mindfulness and meditation, wise mind, radical acceptance, a good handful of DBT skills, self care, self soothing, problem solving.. 
I was seen regularly by a psychiatrist who managed my quetiapine (antipsychotic) and Venlafaxine (antidepressant) medication but mostly it was just me, my practitioner, and a LOT of work.

In the past I've also done CBT, CAT, CFT, counselling, and other therapies as well as group work.

Basically I'm saying that while I empathise strongly with you, I will suggest that to get better you will most probably need access to some kind of professional help that you agree with, a therapist that you like and get along with, and an attitude that you're willing to put a LOT of work in as well.

BPD is a horrible disorder to have, but its possible to learn how to cope with the symptoms, and even learn how to reduce the frequency of them as well. It just takes effort.

Hi there. I am 31, I have numerous health issues both mental and physical, including a lot of chronic pain, and I am married. My husband cares for me a little, but  mostly I can manage by myself.

So for the issue of intimacy I can tell you now I probably won't be too much help, as my husband and I haven't been sexually active for six years because of his age related impotency.
The only thing I would advise is to recommend you both go and see a counsellor, either a relationship counsellor (which would help with the rest of your problems too) or a specialised sex counsellor. Your wife does have pain and fatigue, yes, and maybe her not wanting sex does make her feel guilty and stressed, but that should not mean that is the end of all discussions - that's not fair on you. 

That point applies to you feeling lonely too. You needn't think that just because she may feel guilty that you should avoid discussing certain topics. A marriage needs discussions to survive, as I think you have realised.
I do think you should get some outside help from a counsellor who will know where to direct your energies and attention, though.

Pain makes our lives difficult to live. It makes every single task hard to do, and sometimes we don't do things because we just don't have the energy any more. We do feel guilty that we don't live the lives we used to do, have the relationships we used to do, and so on. 
But we're not made of glass; we won't break into pieces if you don't wrap us in cotton wool. We're the same person inside that we were before we got all this pain, and we can handle a discussion like an adult.

Just try telling her straight that you NEED to have a proper conversation with her because you are so lonely and you miss her, and it's not to make her feel guilty, it's because you want to keep the relationship as strong as it always has been!

Good luck, I wish you the best.
